As an example, I'll pick one vitamin: the Vitamin A family.

Vitamins actually come in families of compounds that can fulfill the same function. Two forms of "Vitamin A" are retinol (found in animal sources) and the carotenes (found in plants).

Vitamin A is required to do various functions in our bodies, like helping our vision, enabling embryos to grow, and so on. Deficiency leads to major problems.

We can figure how how much Vitamin A we need to eat, but this is not as straightforward as it sounds.

Retinol (animal sourced Vitamin A) is readily absorbed and used by our bodies. Since it comes from an animal, and since we are animals, very little processing is needed by our bodies before we start using it.

The carotenes, on the other hand, are not readily useable. In fact, they're described as Vitamin A precursors, because they have to be modified by our bodies before we can start using it in the same role as retinol.

This conversion happens at a very poor rate.

An early estimate of 6:1 was revised to 12:1 and from recent studies and experimental trials carried out in developing nations it was revised again to 21:1.Sommer A (2008). "Vitamin a deficiency and clinical disease: An historical overview". The Journal of Nutrition. 138 (10): 1835–9. PMID 18806089.

This means you need to eat over twenty times as much carotene to get the same end result in retinol. Utterly wasteful.

Note that this terrible ratio is not reflected on nutrition labels.

Herbivorous animals convert carotenes to retinol at a much higher efficiency. Thus, from an environmental standpoint it's much more ecologically sound to get our retinol from animal sources rather than using over 20x the plants ourselves.

And from here we go on to realize there are a hundred vitamins, minerals, and other compounds we need to eat every day. This same type of argument can be said about vitamin D (from cod livers), vitamin K (found in milk from animals that ate new shoots of spring grass) and so on down the list.
